analysis.one_liner: Strengthens union organizing rights, raises employer penalties, and overrides state right-to-work laws.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 224-194 in February 2020, but the Senate never voted on it and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it easier for workers to form unions and harder for employers to fight them. It would classify more workers as employees (covering many gig workers), ban mandatory arbitration agreements that block group lawsuits, bar employers from forcing workers into anti-union meetings, let unions collect fees from all workers in a unit even in states that ban it, and raise penalties on lawbreaking employers to as much as $100,000 per violation with a new right to sue. It passed the House but died without a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize or join a union gain the most: employers could no longer hold mandatory anti-union meetings, permanently replace strikers, or use arbitration clauses to block class-action suits, and penalties for firing or retaliating against organizing workers would rise sharply. Gig workers classified as independent contractors would be covered by labor law under a new test. Unions gain bargaining rights, access to worker contact lists, mandatory arbitration of first contracts, and the ability to collect fair-share fees from all workers in a unit regardless of state right-to-work laws.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers trying to organize and unions

how_it_helps.text: It narrows who counts as a supervisor and applies a new test that treats workers as employees unless they are free from control, doing work outside the employer's main business, and running their own independent business — pulling many gig and contract workers under labor-law protections.

It makes it an unfair labor practice to coerce employees into attending employer meetings aimed at discouraging union membership, and to permanently replace workers who strike or discriminate against those who return from one.
It bans forced arbitration clauses that stop employees from joining class or collective lawsuits, letting workers band together in court.

It raises the stakes for employers who break the law: civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation ($100,000 for repeat violators), back pay with no offset, double liquidated damages, punitive damages in court, and a new private right of action for employees.

It speeds up union elections (hearings within 8 days, elections within 20 business days), requires employers to hand over workers' contact information to the organizing union, strips employers of standing to participate in representation proceedings, and lets the NLRB certify a union without a rerun election if the employer interfered and a majority had signed cards.

It lets collective bargaining agreements require all employees in a unit to pay fees for representation even in states that ban it, permits sympathy (secondary) strikes, and requires binding arbitration of a first contract if mediation fails — so a newly certified union cannot simply be stalled forever.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost: businesses organizing targets would face faster elections with no employer participation, mandatory arbitration of first contracts, higher fines, exposure to class actions, and lawsuits from individual workers. Franchise brands would risk being treated as joint employers of franchisee workers, and gig platforms would have to treat many drivers as employees. Unionized businesses would also see sympathy strikes legalized against them. Some costs could be passed to consumers in prices, and employees who oppose unionization would have to pay fair-share fees or accept organizing activity on the job.

drawbacks.text: If a newly certified union and the employer cannot agree on a first contract, a three-member arbitration panel would impose a binding two-year contract using factors like the employer's finances and workers' cost of living — taking the final terms out of both sides' hands, which critics say can impose unaffordable terms on struggling businesses.

The fair-share provision would override state right-to-work laws and require every employee in a covered bargaining unit to pay union fees as a condition of employment, including workers who voted against unionization or choose not to join.

Employers would lose standing to participate in NLRB representation proceedings over their own employees and would have to hand over workers' home addresses, phone numbers, and emails to the organizing union within two business days, raising privacy and due-process concerns the bill only partially addresses with a rule of construction.

Penalties up to $50,000-$100,000 per violation, double liquidated damages, and a new private right of action would substantially raise the cost of doing business and litigation risk for employers, including small businesses that may face organizing campaigns.
Legalizing secondary strikes would allow unions to pressure neutral businesses that are not the direct employer in a dispute, exposing bystander firms and their workers to pickets and work stoppages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers trying to organize, the bill addresses the main ways employer resistance stalls unions today: captive-audience meetings, lengthy election delays, stall-and-punish tactics during first-contract bargaining, and penalties so small they are treated as a cost of doing business. The trade-offs are real but mostly fall on the employer side: imposed first contracts, fee requirements for non-members, loss of employer participation in elections, and much higher litigation exposure. Critics' strongest points are the binding-arbitration mandate and the override of state right-to-work laws; supporters would answer that current law already lets employers delay indefinitely at little cost.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 224-194, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in May 2019 with 218 cosponsors — 216 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
The House Education and Labor Committee approved an amended version by a vote of 26-21 in September 2019 and formally reported it that December.
On February 6, 2020, the House rejected a Republican motion to recommit 195-223 and passed the bill 224-194, with 219 of 226 voting Democrats in favor and only 5 of 191 voting Republicans.

The Senate received the bill on February 10, 2020 and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it received no further action and expired at the end of the 116th Congress in January 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the new organizing rules — particularly large nonunion employers, gig platforms, and franchisors — are better off because the bill never reached a Senate vote, leaving federal labor law as it was.

for.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
for.role: Sponsor; Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, guided it through committee markup (approved 26-21), and reported it to the floor.

for.name: House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Supplied 219 of the bill's 224 votes for passage and 216 of its 218 cosponsors.

for.name: Labor unions (AFL-CIO and affiliated unions)
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for the bill as their top legislative priority.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for Senate action after it arrived from the House; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted 186-5 against passage and offered the motion to recommit and amendments against the bill.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business groups
against.what_they_did: Ran a major campaign against the bill, arguing it would raise costs for employers and override state right-to-work laws.

against.name: President Trump
against.what_they_did: The administration issued a statement of opposition saying his advisors would recommend a veto.

sides.party_line_note: In the House, 219 of 226 voting Democrats supported the bill while only 5 of 191 voting Republicans did, and the failed motion to recommit split almost entirely by party as well (192 of 195 yes votes were Republicans); 2 Republicans cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill is the largest expansion of union power in decades: easier elections, imposed first contracts, fair-share fees, legal sympathy strikes, and immunity for unions from employer lawsuits over secondary strikes. Unions would gain members, dues, and leverage.

industries.industry: Gig economy platforms (ride-hailing, delivery, freelance marketplaces)
industries.note: The new test would reclassify many drivers and gig workers as employees covered by labor law, ending their independent-contractor business model and forcing them to treat workers as employees.

A broad joint-employer definition would make franchisors and other intermediaries co-employers when they share control over workers' conditions, exposing brands to bargaining and liability at franchisee locations.

Penalties up to $50,000-$100,000 per violation, a private right of action, banned captive meetings, faster elections with no employer participation, and binding first-contract arbitration would raise the cost and risk of fighting or managing unions.

industries.industry: Union-avoidance consultants and persuader law firms
industries.note: The bill narrows the exemption that lets consultants avoid public disclosure of anti-union campaigns, requiring reporting for planning meetings, training supervisors, and drafting anti-union communications.
